standard.title: Roles of government
standard.description: the roles and responsibilities of the 3 levels of government in Australia
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS4K08 (Local government and services): Students explain that local government provides specific services to communities. From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students know that elected representatives exist at different levels of government.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government in Australia — local, state/territory and federal — and understand how their responsibilities interact and sometimes overlap.

nodes.label: Three levels and their primary responsibilities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name the three levels of government and describe the primary roles and responsibilities of each level.
nodes.minimum_width: Name the three levels of government and describe at least two responsibilities of each.
nodes.typical_width: Sort and categorise the roles and responsibilities of local (roads, rubbish, parks, local planning), state/territory (schools, hospitals, police, state roads, public transport) and federal (defence, immigration, foreign affairs, social security, national laws) governments.
wider: Investigate the specific responsibilities of your local council and compare them with the responsibilities of your state government — identifying what is managed at each level and why
Examine a local community issue and identify which level of government is primarily responsible for addressing it, explaining the reasoning
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear map of which level is responsible for what, students cannot analyse overlapping responsibilities, resolve confusion about who is accountable for specific issues, or understand how the federal system operates.

response_modes.reason: Use a sorting activity (card sort or three-column table) to categorise responsibilities across the three levels — make the categories concrete before moving to analysis of overlap and interaction.

success_criteria: Students name the three levels of government.
Students correctly categorise at least two responsibilities for each level.

nodes.label: Overlapping powers and constitutional hierarchy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify issues where multiple levels of government have overlapping powers, and explain that federal law overrides state law when they conflict on these issues.
nodes.minimum_width: Give one example of an area where federal and state governments both have the power to make laws, and explain what happens if they conflict.
nodes.typical_width: Identify areas of concurrent legislative power (e.g. environment, education, health) where federal and state parliaments both make laws; explain that federal law overrides state law when they conflict on concurrent issues; give examples of this happening.
wider: Investigate the Murray-Darling Basin water management as an example of multiple levels of government involvement, and evaluate the challenges of managing a shared resource across state and federal jurisdictions
Research a specific case where federal and state laws have conflicted on an environmental or social issue, and trace how the conflict was resolved

response_modes.reason: Concurrent powers and federal override are abstract constitutional concepts — students need concrete case examples (environment, Murray-Darling) to understand how the constitutional hierarchy operates in practice.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Murray-Darling Basin example is a rich and current case of multi-level government interaction with genuine complexity — examining it provides real depth in understanding how the federal system manages shared environmental resources.
success_criteria: Students give at least one example of overlapping federal and state powers.
Students explain that federal law overrides state law in cases of conflict.

nodes.label: How new laws originate
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how new laws originate in Australia, including from party policy, member or senator proposals, and interest group advocacy.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe two ways new laws can originate in Australia.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how new laws can originate: from party policy (announced during election campaigns), from suggestions by members and senators, and from interest groups and community organisations lobbying government — and trace the pathway a new law typically follows from idea to legislation.
wider: Investigate the passage of a specific piece of Australian legislation from its origins to its passing, tracing the individuals, groups and processes involved
Examine a community campaign that successfully led to new legislation, and assess what made the campaign effective

response_modes.reason: The law-making process involves multiple stages and actors — use a flowchart of the legislative process to make the sequence visible before students analyse how it works in specific cases.

success_criteria: Students describe at least two sources of new law proposals.
Students explain one step in the pathway from proposal to legislation.

nodes.label: The three-level system in practice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government, identify where responsibilities interact or overlap, and give examples of how each level makes and enforces laws in their community.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain the roles of all three levels and give one example from daily life of each level's responsibility.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the responsibilities of local, state/territory and federal government; identify overlapping responsibilities in at least one area; describe the types of laws and regulations each level makes and who enforces them (e.g. road laws, health laws, pollution laws); connect to real examples from their own community.
wider: Map all three levels of government involvement in one community issue (e.g. environmental management, housing, transport) and evaluate whether the division of responsibilities is effective
Evaluate whether there are areas where the current distribution of responsibilities between levels could be improved, and propose a change with justification

response_modes.reason: The integration challenge is connecting the abstract framework (three levels, their roles) to concrete community reality (specific laws, services, enforcement). Local examples are essential for making the abstract system visible.

success_criteria: Students correctly describe the primary responsibilities of all three levels of government.
Students give one real-life example of each level's responsibility from their own community.
Students explain how governments at different levels interact on at least one issue.
